items.title: Show HN: Gall – Inkling 2 Mini on 24GB M2, frees RAM between messages
items.description:
Show HN: Thinking Machines Lab gives 32GB as the minimum RAM requirement for Inkling 2 Mini on Mac, but with the Q3 quant I felt it must be possible to get somewhere reasonable on my 24GB M2 MacBook Air. Llama.cpp wasn't cutting it even with patches, so I spent this week's Fable allowance (with a sprinkling of Astra) on this custom inference engine, and took the opportunity to add some optimisations and ergonomics for running on a memory-constrained laptop: - strictly one model loaded at a time, requests queued; - KV cache gets saved and model unloaded after every response (or configurable delay), so RAM stays at 50MB between calls, but reload is fast; - menu bar app shows status and icon changes when prefilling/generating. So far I've been using it with hax [1] with my normal system prompt + tool list, which runs to about 2,800 tokens, and getting near-instant responses in new sessions due to the cache-and-reload. Works great as a local agent setup for infrequent messages too, e.g. via a Telegram bridge. I'm sure this vibecoded engine and the model itself will be superseded in time, but for now it's by far the best local model setup I've ever managed on this machine, so wanted to share for others in the same boat. Please do hack away at it. 1. https://github.com/OleksandrChekhovskyi/hax
Website metadata: A from-scratch Metal inference engine for Inkling 2 Mini on Apple silicon - ltrgoddard/gall

items.title: Show HN: Type-C – variants, options, generics and pattern matching for C
items.description:
Show HN: I love C, but often using it for parsing, tree walking or complex error handling leads to spaghetti code. Of course there is Swift, Ocaml or Rust for situations like that, but then you are either forced to convert the entire codebase, or add a runtime library or go through the pain of bridging C to the new language. Sometimes there are no compilers for the target architecture too when you are working on embedded stuff. This is where Type-C comes in. It works as a preprocessor like TypeScript and calls the original C driver behind the scenes. Your code stays normal C for the most part, so you can predict how the code will be laid out. TypeC is a full superset of C11, so any C11 code compiles as is. Want to use TypeC just for one file? Rename to .tc and use the features you want, the rest of the codebase stays the same. This works for kernel or baremetal code too as there is no runtime or extra libararies. There are examples of TypeC code as well as real-world tests of converting existing code to TypeC on the GitHub page. This is how the code looks like for an expression evaluator: type expr = | Num(int value) | Add(const expr l, const expr r) | Mul(const expr l, const expr r) | Div(const expr l, const expr r); static result(int, eval_error) eval(const expr *e) { int d; match (*e) { case Num(value): return (Ok(value)); case Add(l, r): return (fit((long long)try eval(l) + try eval(r))); case Mul(l, r): return (fit((long long)try eval(l) * try eval(r))); case Div(l, r): d = try eval(r); if (d == 0) return (Err(DivByZero)); return (fit((long long)try eval(l) / d)); } } % typec -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra eval.tc $ ./a.out 14 division by zero Would love to hear your thoughts and feedback!
Website metadata: C11 with the types C is missing: variants, options, generics and exhaustive matching - stass/type-c

items.title: Show HN: Rmux – A lightweight GPU rendered terminal workspace
items.description:
Show HN: Hey HN, I've been working on rmux, an open source terminal workspace built in Rust using GPUI and Ghostty's terminal engine. The main focus has been performance. I wanted something that could handle multiple projects, shells and coding agents without becoming a resource hog or feeling sluggish as more panes are opened, which has been a frustration I've had with some other terminals. I also have a sweet setup for it to be my standard external terminal for VS Code where I can switch back and forth between the same workspace in VS Code and rmux with a single shortcut. I share the details of how that's done on the VS Code page on the website. It supports named workspaces, tabs, split panes, keyboard shortcuts and a command palette. Nothing particularly revolutionary in terms of features, but the goal is to make the experience as responsive and lightweight as possible. Of course the site has a WASM demo - because it's in Rust and that's what the cool people do. Would be interested to hear what people think, particularly around performance and the overall UX. Source is on GitHub, linked from the website.
Website metadata: A native terminal workspace built for responsiveness. Rust, GPU rendering and Ghostty, with split panes and project workspaces.

items.title: Show HN: It's now easy to install Linux on an Android Phone – Android2linux
items.description:
Show HN: Hey HN! One of my biggest dreams (really) was to have a Linux phone. I tried to install on some phones in the past, even the ones that would be marked as compatible and it was always so difficult that I couldn't really do it. Yesterday I decided to try again, this time using Claude to do most of the work. A couple hours later it runs postmarketOS as my second phone: 4G, SMS, a terminal, SSH. It took two fixes. U-Boot didn't recognise my phone model, so I patched 14 bytes of its device-tree match strings. Then the modem wasn't working, because the packaged TFTP server that lends the modem a folder mishandled its file-size queries but an upstream build fixed it. The repo is what came out of it: guides for any phone (but specific just for my xiaomi), an agent skill that follows the same method and safety rules, notes per phone, and web apps reworked for a phone screen (WhatsApp Web for desktop with a one-pane layout). What doesn't work (in this phone of mine): no charger driver yet (slow charging), no cameras, and no banking apps, so I keep an Android at home for those. Whether this works for you depends on your phone having a port. reports through the issue forms help, especially for phones that don't work yet. I think that finally succeeding at having a Linux phone is worth creating a post on HN. I was thinking about a Tell HN but decided to convert the knowledge into a repo so more people can share, discuss, add their phones, new apps, etc. Hope it helps!
Website metadata: Turn an Android phone into a Linux pocket computer you control: guides, an agent skill, phone notes, scripts and apps for postmarketOS and Ubuntu Touch. - android2linux/android2linux
items.product_description: Turn an Android phone into a Linux pocket computer you control: guides, an agent skill, phone notes, scripts and apps for postmarketOS and Ubuntu Touch. - android2linux/android2linux

items.description:
Show HN: I built it because it's very hard to keep up with all the new CVEs coming out. The main problem is I don't know which ones apply to my computer, projects or our infra. So I built pantry to make it easier to figure out what actually needs to be patched, if it even can be, and how to do it quickly. items.description:
Show HN: Almost two and a half years ago, I had an idea for a game where you program Python bots to battle each other. Today I'm finally sharing it with you all (which is a little nerve-wracking): https://bashbots.io On the site, you can watch bashes (battles between bots), browse the equipment upgrades, check out packages other players have published, read the operations manual, and start writing code in the editor. Creating and running your own bot needs a free account (email, Google, or GitHub), since bots run on the server. The full site is built for desktop, and mobile has bashes and the manual. If you'd like a walkthrough, I made a short video series on building your first bot: https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLdIHqbLcMqVI If you want a challenge, see if you can beat my own bot: https://bashbots.io/bots/b33-p I'd love to hear what you all think.
